Honors Community One of the hallmarks of honors education is the community that emerges from a shared experience featuring intense student-to-stu- dent and mentor-to-student interaction in an engaging learning environment.
While honors students establish affinity with many different groups on campus, the connection to honors is often one of the earliest because they enter the institution as part of an honors cohort and first encounter campus as a matriculated student in an honors orientation.
Like student-athletes, for example, honors students self-select into a program with distinct characteristics at the start of their college careers, which strengthens bonds across the group.
These features position honors as a potential hub on campus that may connect many different units – academic and co-curric- ular – because honors students tend to be drawn from all majors.
As a result, the institution supports this community by providing adequate financial, physical, and personnel resources. • Honors orientation programming is used to established community early in honors students’ careers but also does not take place in isolation.

Such programming provides opportunities to bring different units across campus together in support of stu- dent engagement, for example in a service project serving the institution’s local community or via City as Text™ programming.
Student Professional Development Honors programs and colleges provide professional development opportunities for students, thereby supporting a wide array of admin- istrative tasks, raising the visibility of honors, and improving programs in ways that remain authentic to students. • Honors student leaders may be called on to help recruit prospective students, serve on faculty and staff search committees, interact with donors, design co-curricular and social programming, and serve as peer mentors, among many other activities.

Infrastructure & Resources Personnel and Budgetary Resources The permanence and stability of an honors program or college is ensured through adequate infrastructure and resources, including an appropriate budget as well as appropriate faculty, professional staff, and administrative support when necessary. • Honors does not depend on the good will and energy of particular faculty members or administrators for survival; instead, the program is fully institutionalized so that it can build a lasting tradition of inclusive excellence.
Program Fees While some honors programs or colleges may employ additional fees to participate in honors, such practices limit access and equity. • Such programs may wish to consider scholarship waivers for low-income students and be cognizant that such fees may signal that honors spaces are more welcoming to privileged students.

NCHC Shared Principles and Practices 7 Honors Advising In acknowledgment of their need to satisfy requirements for multiple programs, honors students receive honors-related academic advising from qualified faculty and/or professional staff.
Additionally, when appropriate to the institutional culture, priority enrollment is provided to active honors students in recognition of the scheduling difficulties caused by the need to satisfy both honors and major program requirements, as is often the case with other distinctive populations like student athletes or student veterans. • Advisors are trained in and employ inclusive-based advising strategies so that rather than serving as mere sources of informa- tion they can provide student-centered growth opportunities to a diverse body of students.
Honors Spaces Like all units on campus, honors programs and colleges best cultivate a distinct identity and serve their diverse populations with appro- priate physical spaces.
Such designated locations are especially important to honors programs and colleges because their students are drawn from majors across campus and because of the important role they often play in recruiting.

As a result, the institution provides adequate, accessible, and inclusive spaces that are welcoming to all honors students, faculty, professional staff, and administration. • One such communal space might include residential facilities—where appropriate to the institution—in which honors stu - dents are housed together and receive honors-designed curricular and co-curricular programing like Living-Learning Com- munities; and in the form of classroom spaces that are well-aligned with honors pedagogy (for example, seminar rooms that best serve discussion-based honors courses). • While some honors programs may be able to establish community without dedicated space, the wide variety of opportunities detailed in the NCHC monograph Housing Honors suggest the many advantages of creating locations for members of the honors community to interact.
For programs and colleges with significant commuter populations, attention is paid to creating spaces that allow such students to feel connected to campus and the honors community.

Alumni Engagement Because graduates often have a strong affinity for the honors program or college and its community, honors programs and colleges typically engage in robust alumni outreach through an advisory board and other mechanisms.
Advisory boards may be involved in advocacy, alumni engagement, fundraising, student mentoring, and recruitment, among other activities. • Honors advisory boards not only provide excellent opportunities to enhance engagement with honors graduates but they provide an opportunity for the institution to vet potential candidates for other alumni-related leadership opportunities like the Board of Trustees, Foundation Board, or Alumni Board.
An abridged version of NCHC’s Shared Principles and Practices is also available.

Considering the Honors Contract as an Effective Tool for Furthering Honors Education at URI SUMMARY This document briefly explores the concept of honors contracts, formal agreements facilitated by an honors program, uniting students and instructors to enhance non-honors courses to an hon- ors level through additional work tailored to the “broader, deeper and more complex” learning experiences advocated by the National Collegiate Honors Council (NCHC).
Contracts are recog- nized by over 60% of honors programs in the USA, where they foster community and ownership, enhancing the educational process and commitment to the programs’ success.
Successful honors contracts depend on effective setup, management, and assessment at the hon- ors administration level.
Customization to students’ and faculty interests is essential, providing personalized educational journeys and one-on-one time with instructors.
Students looking to set up contracts should follow a structured approach, guided by honors administration.

This could include early communication about opportunities, advising to educate students on the process and benefits, and encouraging them to approach advisors when identify- ing contract possibilities.
Initiating the process involves engaging with faculty, guided by advis- ing, before registration.
Detailed contracts specifying the project, its outcomes, deadlines, and contact schedules, ensure clarity.
Faculty handle grading, with the honors organization approving credits.
Contracts should bridge the gap between honors and non-honors classrooms, maintaining high standards and clear expectations.
To ensure the effectiveness of honors contracts, too routine or casual use must be prevented.
They should complement, not replace, the program’s curriculum, while preserving community and support.
Faculty involvement should be incentivized and re- warded to maintain a dynamic and successful contract system.

Honors contracts provide flexibility for students to align their education with their interests and goals and allow programs to meet student needs when constraints of students or faculty numbers or funding limitations do not allow honors courses to be run that answer to their interests and needs.
This empowers students, fosters motivation, and facilitates mentor-mentee relationships with faculty. ~KA NOTES ON HONORS CONTRACTS KARL ASPELUND, ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR, URI HONORS OCTOBER 23, 2023

WHAT IS AN HONORS CONTRACT?
AN HONORS CONTRACT is a signed agreement between a student and in- structor.
Facilitated by the honors program, the contract states that the student will complete a specified project in addition to other coursework required and thus “convert” the non-honors class to an honors-equivalent course through additional work, such as outside reading, independent research, or some other enhanced learning activity (Badenhausen, 7).
Usually, students are required to earn both an A or B grade for the regular coursework and submit acceptable contract work to qualify for honors credit. (James, 30) A little over 60% of honors programs in the USA—regardless of institutional type—use contracts (Bahls, 172.) CONTRACTS provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility at institutions that are not able to field enough faculty, cannot provide an adequate number of honors courses, or do not have a large enough of a student body to fill hon- ors sections.
Contracts can fill the gap and provide opportunities for students’ self-guided intellectual growth (Bahls, 175).

For example, work at the University Honors Program at the University of Kan- sas shows that honors contracts act as far more than stopgaps to address honors course shortages.
They can “facilitate access to honors, increase completion, democratize key aspects of the honors experience, provide students with struc- tured avenues for building relationships with faculty members, and empower students to own their educational experiences” (Dotter, 56).
Honors contracts not only maximize faculty-student contact in classes of any format, they also accommodate exploration and questioning in a range of research disciplines, from team-taught humanities discussions to innovative in- vestigations in STEM courses, including their labs (Myers and Whitebread, 22.) Further, as a valued part of honors education, tutorial-based contracts can be seen as a special approach used in various modes of learning: Research and creative scholarship, breadth and enduring questions, service learning and leadership, experiential learning, and learning communities.

They can therefore similarly result in the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learner-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors educa- tion (Myers and Whitebread, 40 & NCHC Shared Principles and Practices).
WHY USE HONORS CONTRACTS?
Provide an extra measure of curricular flexibility Empower students to their own learning experiences Maximize faculty-student contact Result in broader, deeper, and more complex learning centered and learner direct- ed experiences An agreement, mediated by the honors program, be- tween student and instructor that defines further work that“converts” the non-hon- ors class to an honors equivalent course. 60+ % of programs use contracts 2 Honors education is characterized by in-class and extracurricular activities that are measurably broader, deeper, or more complex than comparable learn - ing experiences typically found at institutions of higher education.

Honors expe - riences include a distinctive learner-directed environment and philosophy, pro - vide opportunities that are appropriately tailored to fit the institution’ s culture and mission, and frequently occur within a close community of students and faculty. ~National Collegiate Honors Council: Definition of Honors Education

HOW ARE CONTRACTS SET UP EFFECTIVELY?
A COMPREHENSIVE SET OF GUIDELINES, that include the basic expecta- tions of the honors experience and specific expectations for contracting, should be available and presented to students early on.
These should include that two of the primary purposes of contracting are to: 1) enable a student and faculty member to establish a one-to-one, ongoing mentor-mentee relationship through- out the semester and 2) to enable the student to experience the subject matter in more depth. (Bolsch, 54) Three honors-related dissertations reporting mixed experiences with contracts find or imply that students appreciate contracts when they meet two conditions: 1) student and faculty customize the work to fit a student’s interests, and 2) con- tracts involve significant time with the instructor (Myers and Whitebread: 23) Faculty members should be solely responsible for assigning course grades.
However, the contracting process should be structured from the outset as one in which the honors organization certifies that a successfully contracted course should be designated for “honors credit” on a student’s transcript.

So, while the faculty member assigns the grade for the course based on requirements unrelat- ed to the contract, honors administration is responsible for placing, essentially, a “seal of approval” on each contract experience through an additional transcript notation once it receives the faculty member’s certification that the elements of the contract were completed. (See: Bolsch, 52) Creating databases for honors advisors of all past digital contracts, searchable by course and faculty mentor’s name can lead to more proactive advising about innovative approaches to contracts and increased access to examples before students even meet with faculty. (Thomas & Hunter, 242) THE A V AILABILITY AND BENEFITS OF CONTRACTS need to be careful- ly publicized to newly-arrived honors students.
Honors advisors should initially help students understand where in their trajec- tory an honors contract might be instrumental and beneficial.
It should be made clear how important a dialogue with instructors will be, and how much this relies on student initiative and their own vision for their learning.

Honors administration and advisors should promote that students, immediate- ly on identifying a course within which they´d be interested to do contracted work, that they talk with an honors advisor to ensure that they understand the process and are aware of their options. “These meetings allow students to re- hearse future conversations with faculty in a safe environment, enable advisors to set clear expectations for contracts, and equip students with the necessary language to meet those expectations” (Dotter, 59.) Students should approach instructors before registering to discuss options and get a firm commitment so the contract is viable and that the honors credits they are receiving that term will be sufficient for their continuing success.
HOW SHOULD STUDENTS APPROACH SETTING UP A CONTRACT?
Searchable databases of past digital contracts lead to more proactive advising Publicize contracts early and often!
Encourage students to ap- proach advisors as soon as they see an opportunity for a contract arise.

Students must approach faculty—with the help of ad- vising— before registering to begin the process Two primary purposes: Enabling a mentor-mentee relationship and a more in-depth experience of the subject matter Students appreciate con- tracts that are fitted to their interests and afford signifi- cant time with the instructor Faculty assign grades, the honors organization ap- proves the honors credits and notifies Enrollment Services.
Advise students early on about the process and bene- fits of contracts 3
WHAT MIGHT A CONTRACT STIPULATE?

FIVE COMPONENTS should be, at least, required for a contract: 1) A substantial (15-20 p.) paper or project (of equivalent time/effort: c. 20 hours) should be defined and outlined. 2) It should be required that the student share the knowledge/skills/experienc- es gained through the paper or project with an audience, either in the class or elsewhere. 3) The contract should include a plan for how the faculty member and student have regular contact outside of class to discuss the student’s progress and an- swer questions regarding the paper or project. 4)The student should be required to state specifically on the contract form how they will meet each of the three NCHC requirements of “broader, deeper, more complex.” 5) A date at the midpoint of the semester should be determined at which the faculty member should provide a brief report to honors administration on the contact they have had with the student and assess the student’s progress to date. (See: Bolsch 2005: 55) CONTRACTS EXEMPLIFY THE BEST OF HONORS PEDAGOGY when, anchored in the tutorial model, they cultivate personalized, mentored learning and ensure consistent, documented quality (Myers and Whitebread, 22).

It is therefore important that honors administrators and advisors keep a close eye on the contracts created, their implementation, and progress, and provide solid templates and rubrics for their creation and use.
While contract courses do not always provide a venue for honors students to interact with each other, they do create space for students to collaborate with instructors and develop important mentoring relationships (Wyatt, 215).
This outcome–a “win-win” if well managed–must be continually emphasized to both faculty and students.
An inclusive pedagogical practice opens the curriculum to a wide array of fac- ulty who become stakeholders in honors.
It has been shown that these curricular practices have led to greater acceptance of and appreciation for honors colleges on campuses where faculty participation is widespread (Wyatt, 196).
Honors administration must therefore constantly work toward an awareness of these practices among all faculty at the University, whether they teach honors students or not.
WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSITIVE OUT- COMES FROM THE USE OF CONTRACTS?

Contracts must be well managed and assessed at the honors admin. level so that they be the effective tool that they are.
Contracts foster and sup- port a sense of community and ownership around hon- ors programs.
The contract should define the contracted project, its deliverables and intended outcomes and deadlines, as well as points of contact and required feedback by the faculty supervisor.
Maintain the awareness that contracts are a venue for meaningful student-faculty relationships. 4

WHAT ARE EXAMPLES OF POSSIBLE PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR WHEN USING CONTRACTS AND WHAT ARE PATHS TOW ARD AVOIDING THEM?
PROBLEMS THAT APPEAR ARE NOT INSURMOUNTABLE.
Mostly they are cir- cumvented by a continuing awareness of processes and a care for good structures and assessment, creating contracts that enhance rather than concede the honors experience (Bambina, 122).
Contracts must not become “routine” or commonplace, no matter what their number.
Nor can they become a “secret fix” only available to those “in the know.” The narrow definition of honors programs can lead to charges of elitism and segre- gation if honors students, who increasingly tend to be upper-middle-class, white, and female, become insulated from the general student population in an honors curricular bubble.
The contract approach mitigates this by allowing students to learn in an in- clusive campus-wide environment while still engaging in an honors curriculum and community (Wyatt, 196).
Overworked instructors may agree to contracts but then require little more than comple- tion of extra assignments with minimal instructor-student interaction.

Honors educators have the responsibility to eliminate underdeveloped honors contracts that dilute rather than enrich the academic experiences of students. (Wyatt, 195.) It is good practice for evaluation and assessment templates to be created and provided by the honors organiza- tion.
And oversight of contracts by honors administrators must therefore be well-struc- tured, mandated, and clear, and guidelines must be provided to faculty on deadlines and assessment rubrics.
It is essential that contracted work not simply be “more”; rather, it must be meaningful- ly integrated in each case with the course content and learning goals and the work the course already requires. (Bahls, 177) The contract must therefore measurably outline work that leads to the “broader, deeper, and more complex learning-centered and learn- er-directed experiences” with which the NCHC defines honors education (NCHC).

The suggestion that the learning experience of a contracted class is equivalent to a stand-alone honors class—seeing as the student receives academic credit for both— opens honors programs and colleges up to potential exploitation by administrators who may not see the need for assigning appropriate resources to honors or may even try to cut budgets. (Badenhausen, 11) It must therefore be agreed—and practiced—that when options are limited, contracts are a workable path to honors completion that benefits both the students and the institution, not a work-around for the program or institution to avoid curriculum development and creating classes.
But even though the close community of students and faculty that defines honors edu- cation is achieved here by other means, the importance of achieving a sense of belong- ing to the larger cohort should not be ignored.
Therefore, a stricture should be in place that students be limited in the number of credits they can complete through contracts, especially in their freshman and sophomore years.

Finally, with increasing demands and tightening budgets overburdening faculty with unpaid work that is not recognized in reviews, it is essential that faculty be recognized and compensated for the additional work a contract entails.
Otherwise, faculty fatigue may set in and departments and colleges may resent the outside burdens (Bambina, 118).
The equivalent of a one-credit independent study would seem reasonable, and perhaps an amendment to faculty contracts might state the value of this work for pro- motion and tenure reviews.
Contracts bring honors students into non-honors classrooms, mitigating the separation of honors stu- dents from others.
Contracts are a beneficial part of the honors methods in individual cases, not a substitute for the program.
Students should be a part of an honors cohort, con- tacts should not be allowed to separate them from the group.
Administration must take care to never let contracts become routine or a “secret fix.” Honors admin. must work diligently to maintain high standards, and clear expec- tations Contract-work must mea- surably achieve NCHC goals: broader, deeper, and more complex learning experiences.
Faculty must be rewarded for the work they do, lest fatigue or resentment under- mine the contract system. 5

NOTES ON DISTINGUISHED HONORS FACULTY FELLOWS DRAFT 01, February 13th 2024 These notes are largely based on—and inspired by—the National Collegiate Honors Council’s “Shared Principles and Practices of Honors Education.” Honors faculty are selected based on their preparation for and commitment to the pedagogy and curriculum of the program or college, their ability to provide intellectual leadership and mentoring for diverse students, and willingness to support the mission of honors.
Selection processes help support the hiring of faculty and professional staff who have been historically underrepresented in higher education, as noted in NCHC’s Diversity and Inclusion Statement. (NCHC Shared Principles and Practices of Honors Education, 5) The Honors Program at URI is designed to support students and faculty in exploring innovative teaching methods.
The interdisciplinary nature of Honors, along with students' self-selection into a challenging and exploratory program, makes it an ideal space for educational innovation.
The program encourages faculty to engage in scholarship on novel educational practices, aligning with the National Collegiate Honors Council's (NCHC) guidelines.

We aim to collaborate with the Office for Advancement of Teaching and Learning (ATL) to assist faculty in developing creative and effective teaching strategies and supporting them in providing intellectual leadership and mentorship to diverse students.
Honors faculty will be chosen based on their commitment to the program's pedagogy and curriculum.
Selected faculty will be asked to participate in–and contribute to–sessions fostering collaboration, sharing ideas, and exploring high-impact practices.
The focus will be on aligning classroom and curriculum-building skills with the goals of URI's Honors Program and the best practices outlined by the NCHC.
The Honors Program, guided by the NCHC, emphasizes student focus, individual development, and leadership skills, prompting faculty discussions on tailoring the student experience to encourage students to take responsibility for their direction and productivity in learning.
This involves, among other things, incorporating hands-on experiences, fostering liberal arts skills, and promoting student success across disciplines.

Recognizing students' diverse backgrounds and learning differences, portions of the workshops will focus on cultural competency and inclusive pedagogies.
In line with NCHC recommendations, Distinguished Faculty Fellows will ensure the representation of historically underserved populations in course materials.
Workshops will investigate inclusive teaching practices in course design, syllabus construction, classroom climate, learning activities, and assessment methods.
Faculty will be encouraged to incorporate diversity, equity, inclusion, and global understanding into their courses, and to engage students in community-based learning and research into local manifestations of global issues.

The Honors Program will be assessed regularly.
Given this, workshops will include a brief introduction to program assessment methods, and help faculty align their courses with the Honors Program’s learning outcomes.
Sessions will also delve into the history and purpose of honors programs, as well as the URI Honors Program's strategic plan and core values.
Faculty will explore incorporating these elements into their courses with a disciplinary focus.
HONORS FACULTY FELLOWS We will initiate a cohort of Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows, excellent instructors who strive to be exemplary student-focused educators.
Selection Process There will be different pathways that lead to the nomination of a teacher to become a Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow.
For example, for specific needs, we will reach out directly to a department for suggestions on who might be qualified and available to teach a needed course.
We will also have general needs for courses that meet our program requirements, at which point we will send out a call for nominations to deans and department chairs.

We will publicly announce the newest Distinguished Faculty Fellows at our annual Distinguished Fellows Dinner to be held every spring.
The nomination process will occur twice a year to coincide with the annual review process – in February for tenure-stream faculty members, and in April for teaching-professor-stream faculty.
Each chosen Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow will serve one three-year term, renewable upon mutual agreement and successful completion of the first term.

Department/College nomination Nominations to become a Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow will be made by department chairs and deans and they should be based on the following criteria: ● teaching excellence awards (not mandatory but certainly preferred) ● high average IDEA evaluations in the category of “Progress on Relevant Objectives” ● strong annual review teaching dossier, including, if possible, classroom observations ● nomination by the department, supported by the dean Interest letter and interview Once a faculty member has been nominated by their department and college dean, we will ask the faculty member: 1) to submit an interest letter and CV; 2) meet the Honors administrative team for an interview; 3) to submit a course proposal that adheres to the following guidelines: ● It meets the 4 Honors program outcomes tied to: creative problem solving, social innovation, interconnection and policy advocacy. ● It echoes the best practices in Honors course design as set forth by the NCHC.. ● It is a course proposal that meets the curricular needs of the Honors program.
Privileges

Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows will: ● Become part of an exclusive cohort of distinguished teaching faculty at URI. ● Teach the best students at the University in small-section courses. ● Bring the revenue generated from HPR or H-section courses back to home department and college ● Participate with other distinguished faculty in Distinguished Honors Teaching Studios held throughout the year. ● Be valued by URI’s Provost through the teaching section of their annual review. ● Receive annual recognition of fellows both through media and at an annual Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows dinner. ● Receive an annual Stipend of $1500.
Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow will: ● Attend at least one NCHC teaching workshop, organized by the URI Honors Program, prior to teaching first Honors course to share their teaching practices and learn about the latest in NCHC best practices. ● Teach at least one Honors or HPR course per year (or every other year, if department is constrained in terms of resources) ● Attend Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellow meetings. ● Integrate the Honors Colloquium into their course offerings. ● Relay all Honors announcements in their courses.

Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows will be invited to: ● Present their proposed course in at least one “Launch your course” Distinguished Honors Teaching Studio. ● Serve as collaborator at one “Launch your course” Distinguished Honors Teaching Studio ● Present course taught at one “Recap/Revision Studio”; serve as evaluator/collaborator at one “Recap/Revision Studio” ● Become part of the governance and oversight structures of Honors program.
They may, for examples serve on the Honors curriculum committee or on its advisory committee. ● Contribute to the evaluation and review of their Distinguished Honors colleagues. ● Contribute to the Honors Program assessment. ● Contribute to promoting and raising the visibility of the Honors program and the URI Honors Institute. ● Mentor promising junior colleagues to become Distinguished Honors Faculty Fellows Review and evaluation process ● A peer classroom observation during the first year of a. three-year term. ● After the first iteration of a course, a submission will be requested of a brief recap statement on how the course met the stated course objectives and the Honors program objective.

Suggestions will be invited on what could be improved, and what worked well, should be supported with examples of student work ● At the end of a three-year term, Distinguished Honors Faculty will be invited to deliver a presentation of one of their Honors courses at an Honors faculty showcase.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill2025-2026-02 November20,2025 Approved by FSEC8/27/25 Introduced to the Faculty Senateon10/16/25 Highlights reflect changes since the October Introduction Approved by the Officeof Innovation in General Education10/23/25 Proposal: The following language modifications to Chapter 8 of the University Manual (Academic Requirements) would remove partial outcomes from the General Education program.
Partial General Education outcomes were found to be widely misunderstood by both students and faculty, and are not tracked or reported in ECampus.
This change is expected to significantly improve the university's ability to assess the delivery of the General Education program.
Proposed Language: 8.20.12 All General Education courses will assess at least one Student Learning Outcome.

General Education courses that assess two Student Learning Outcomes may do so in the following configurations: Knowledge (Area A) and Competency (Area B) Knowledge (Area A) and Responsibility (Area C) Competency (Area B) and Competency (Area B) Competency (Area B) and Responsibility (Area C) Integration (Area D) and Competency (Area B) Integration (Area D) and Responsibility (Area C) Students must take at a minimum of three (3) credits of courses, or an approved sequence, for each of the twelve (12) assessed Student Learning Outcomes, plus additional courses to complete a minimum of 40 credits of approved General Education courses.
Approved General Education courses must cover at least 1 or 2 Student Learning Outcomes in full.
Partial coverage of an outcome is no longer recognized for outeomes approved on or after 1 January 2026.
After + January 2026, e Current courses with partial outcomes may opt to remove them or upgrade them to full coverage if they undergo a course change process.
Overlap is allowed when a course fulfills two Student Learning Outcomes, but the credits cannot be double counted (within General Education courses) towards the total of 40.
For information on having any requirement waived by proficiency examination see8.20.15.#13-14-21,#15-16-13 8.20.14 Any course that assesses twe (2) at least one (1) of the General Education Student

Learning Outcomes may be submitted to the General Education Committee for approval to fulfill General Education requirements, regardless of that course's place in a major or prerequisites. No college, department, major, minor, or other program or course of study may require a student to choose a specific course to satisfy the General Education requirements, although courses that fulfill requirements or prerequisites for majors which also happen to satisfy General Education requirements can be recommended through advising.Of the courses taken to complete General Education requirements, only up to 12 credits may share the same disciplinary code. An exception to the limit is allowed for the HPR (Honors Program topic) course code. Only courses that fulfill the D1 Student Learning Outcome, Integrate and Apply, may be graded using S/U. Of D1 courses graded S/U, a student may apply only up to 6 credits to the total 40 credits needed to complete the General Education requirements. #13-14-21#15-16-13#16-17-26B,#17-18-23,#20-21-24

On May 10, 2007, the Faculty Senate approved the following amendment to section 8.2 of the Faculty Senate By-Laws (additions are bold underlined italics, deleted language has strikethrough markings): 8.2 Secret mail ballots of the General Faculty shall be conducted either to ratify amendments to the Senate Constitution or to recall Senate actions.
They shall be conducted as follows: The Secretary of the Senate shall distribute a ballot to every eligible member of the faculty following a procedure adopted by the Faculty Senate.
Mail shall include electronic mail.
Two envelopes shall be distributed with the ballot.
One envelope shall bear the word BALLOT, and will be used by the faculty member to enclose and seal his/her ballot.
The second envelope shall be used as an outer mailing envelope.

In order for a ballot to be valid, it must (1) be returned in the two envelopes as outlined above with the outer envelope signed, and (2) be received by the Secretary of the Senate within 15 days after the date on which the ballots were mailed to the faculty by the Secretary of the Senate, except that faculty members absent on official business may record their vote by telegram or radio-telegram addressed to the Secretary of the Senate, in which case the ballot will not be secret, but it must be recorded within the time limit.
The tellers will validate the eligibility of the voter by the outer signed envelope, and then separate inner sealed envelopes from the outer envelope so that the inner envelopes can no longer be identified with the individual voters before opening the inner envelopes and counting the ballots.
The outer envelopes shall be retained separately until the outcome of the referendum shall have been decided.
The names of those faculty members who have returned ballots as identified by the signatures on the outer envelopes shall be made available to any interested party during the 15-day voting period.

At the end of the 15-day referendum period the ballots shall be counted and the results certified to the President of the University and to the Chairperson of the Senate. 8.2 as amended reads as follows: 8.2 Secret mail ballots of the General Faculty shall be conducted either to ratify amendments to the Senate Constitution or to recall Senate actions.

1 Faculty Senate Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report #2003-04-1 Fall 2003 I.
BACKGROUND Starting in the Fall of 2001, a CBUM "Subcommittee" worked on redesigning the University's committee structure.
The group's tasks were: • To eliminate committees that were no longer operational, or had outlived their usefulness; • To remove from the University Manual committees with a scope too narrow to be included in a document containing general rules applying to the university as a whole; • To update the compositions and the charges of University committees in those case in which a discrepancy between "description on paper" and "real-life functioning" had developed; • To make sure that the committees listed in the University Manual as being in charge of certain matters actually are the places where the decisions on the matters specified are made.
A subsidiary task turned out to be replacing the structure of Chapter 5 of the University Manual--a structure which has become rather murky over the years--by a more logical classification of the University's committees.
II.

SOON IN A THEATER NEAR YOU . . . (HOPEFULLY) Several items the CBUM Subcommittee considered are not finalized yet.
They are: • The status of the University Affirmative Action & Equal Opportunity Committee and its Subcommittees on Sexual Harassment and on Racial and Ethnic Harassment.
Following an extensive hiatus, the Affirmative Action Committee has once again met recently.
It and its subcommittees are listed unchanged in the University Manual Chapter 5 Synopsis (see below) under the Presidential Committees; but changes to the present arrangement might be announced shortly. • The status of the BGS Curriculum Committee (5.80.10-13) and the BGS Scholastic Standing Committee (5.81.10-11).
The Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee has been asked to consider, in consultation with ASFCCE, the status of these committees and make recommendations on them to the Faculty Senate if a change is indicated.
For the time being, both committees are listed unchanged among the committees under joint purview of the Faculty Senate and the President.
